blocks.title: Common ion effect
blocks.text: The suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte by adding a common ion to it is called the common ion effect.

Sodium chloride is purified by passing hydrogen chloride gas through brine, a saturated solution of NaCl. Sodium chloride is fully ionised in the solution, NaCl(s) gives Na+(aq) + Cl-(aq), with Kc = [Na+][Cl-] / [NaCl]. HCl also ionises in solution, HCl(g) gives H+(aq) + Cl-(aq). On passing HCl gas the concentration of Cl- increases, so NaCl crystallises out of the solution to maintain the constant value of the equilibrium constant: Na+(aq) + Cl-(aq) gives NaCl(s). The addition of a common ion to the solution of a less soluble electrolyte suppresses its ionisation, and the concentration of the un-ionised species increases, which may come out as a precipitate.

items: The solubility of the less soluble salt KClO3 in water is suppressed by adding the more soluble salt KCl; K+ is the common ion, the ionisation of KClO3 is suppressed and it settles as a precipitate.

The dissociation of the weak acid H2S, H2S gives 2H+ + S2-, is suppressed by adding the stronger acid HCl; H+ is the common ion, H2S is less dissociated in acidic solution, and the low concentration of S2- produced helps to precipitate the basic radicals of the second group in salt analysis.

Adding NH4Cl, a strong electrolyte, to NH3 solution suppresses the concentration of OH- because of the large excess of NH4+ from NH4Cl; the combination is used as the group reagent for the third group basic radicals.

blocks.text: The common ion effect finds extensive applications in qualitative analysis and in the preparation of buffers.

blocks.prompt: Some NaCl solution is added to a saturated solution of AgCl. What happens to [Ag+], and why (Quick Check 9.4b)?
blocks.explanation: The added Cl- is a common ion. The equilibrium AgCl(s) giving Ag+ + Cl- shifts to the left to keep the product [Ag+][Cl-] constant, so silver chloride precipitates and [Ag+] falls: the solubility of AgCl is suppressed by the common ion.

items: A common ion suppresses the ionisation of a weak or sparingly soluble electrolyte: HCl into brine precipitates NaCl; KCl precipitates KClO3; HCl keeps H2S un-ionised (low S2- for group II); NH4Cl lowers OH- in ammonia (group III reagent).
Used in qualitative analysis and in making buffers.
